He has reported on health policy for more than 10 years, writing for Governing magazine, Talking Points Memo, and STAT before joining Vox in 2017. We’re making this story accessible to all readers as a public service. Support our journalism by becoming a member today . The trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children, is laden with painful what-ifs: What if she had more support? What if she had more people to confide in? Could all of this suffering have been avoided? Those are urgent questions, whatever the outcome of this particular case, because millions of women experience postpartum depression. Severe postpartum psychosis may be extremely rare , but every year at least 1 in 8 women who give birth in the US experience some depression symptoms — and that is likely an undercount. A jury will ultimately decide whether or not to convict her for her children’s deaths; by Tuesday morning, the jurors were still unable to reach a unanimous verdict but the judge in the case ordered them to keep deliberating. Their verdict will rest in part on whether they believe that Clancy was in her right mind when she killed her children — the defense does not contest the underlying facts — or whether, as her attorneys are contending, she was experiencing severe psychosis that should render her not culpable for her actions. Clancy’s case has become a national flashpoint for maternal mental health — a gripping courtroom drama that also exposes how new moms’ mental well-being has been neglected by the health system and researchers for years. It’s easy to feel hopeless in the face of such a tragedy, and much of the coverage has — rightly — focused on the gaps it exposed in the system for women getting the care they need. But even now, there’s good reason to feel optimistic. Doctors and health workers across the United States are experimenting with strategies that can improve postpartum mental health care. They have found a secret ingredient that can help new mothers when they are struggling: other moms who have been through the same thing before. “You just had a baby. You’re responsible for a new human life. And it’s really hard to juggle everything in your life,” Dr. Jessica Gaulton, a pediatrician who founded FamilyWell Health, a postpartum mental health support service that incorporates peer coaches into its program, told me. “Oftentimes what women need is just somebody to be there and have their back.” Postpartum depression is a health system problem, a public health problem — but it’s also a deeply personal one. Helping people make connections that make them not feel so alone is one way we can start to improve the postpartum outlook for American mothers. And a wave of local programs — and research showing that they really work — is offering some promising new ideas about how to deliver more compassionate and effective care for postpartum depression. During the Clancy trial, the Maternal Mental Health Alliance has listed five steps that could be taken to improve postpartum care. One of their top priorities is better care coordination among the different healthcare providers who see a new mom after she’s given birth. The so-called “collaborative care model” has been building momentum for years now, since it was first introduced for postpartum care for Medicaid patients in Seattle’s King County more than a decade ago. The model has since spread to other places, but the basic tenet is this: It takes a whole team to care for a new mother and watch out for her mental health, and they need a point person to help manage their care. In Los Angeles, for example, where a group of nonprofits is wrapping up a five-year pilot program based on the collaborative care model, new mothers are assigned to a behavioral-health care manager. The manager performs assessments and brief interventions, works with a psychiatric consultant to continually assess how the patient is doing, and cooperates with the OB/GYN or primary care doctor to manage the patient’s treatment. Rather than waiting for a psychiatrist to have an open appointment when she’s struggling right now, the new mom’s preexisting healthcare providers can step in with support from a mental health professional to manage postpartum depression symptoms. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. In evaluations, the model has consistently outperformed other standards of care in reducing symptoms. But while we have started to see collaborative care spread to other parts of the US, its progress has been halting for various logistical and financial reasons. The Maternal Mental Health Alliance is urging health systems and health insurers to invest in more care coordination programs. And now some providers are building on the collaborative care model with an important new element: peer support. In Washington, the MOMCare program is now experimenting with peer “navigators” to help their patients figure out the appropriate place to get the care they need. In Massachusetts, Gaulton’s FamilyWell Health, which works with OB/GYN practices to provide mental health services, launched a pilot program that added certified behavioral health coaches. These people were recruited because they had their own life experience of giving birth and having postpartum depression symptoms; the coaches were frequently doulas, nurses, and midwives. Patients would talk once or twice a week with their coach to set goals and receive positive feedback, while the coaches had a protocol to follow if it seemed their patient required more serious support. A study published in April found that this new coach-driven approach was successfully reducing depression and anxiety symptoms. Patients experience remission of their depression symptoms within an average of nine days with a peer coach, versus eight days with a licensed therapist. In other words, the mothers assigned to a peer got better almost as quickly as those who saw a professional. Gaulton said she introduced the peer-coach concept to FamilyWell Health because of her own experiences as a new mom. She struggled to recognize her own depression symptoms. When she did, she leaned on a friend and fellow neonatologist at the hospital where she worked for help. Then during Covid, she saw moms with otherwise healthy babies struggling during that world-altering public health emergency. “What I realized was that we were underutilizing coaches,” Gaulton said. “For decades, we’ve been using peer groups, peer coaching in this field to support, but it has never been formalized. There was no formal training.” So she decided to found a new company dedicated to supporting new mothers’ mental health — and she brought those lessons with her. This idea — training experienced moms to help new moms — has been gaining traction across the country. In Colorado, researchers from the University of Colorado launched a program called Alma , which connects new moms with another woman who has been through the same experiences and received specialized training to provide emotional support. The program’s mentors receive 80 hours of training and then meet up to 10 times with a new mother, either in person or virtually, to talk about what makes them feel good and how to incorporate it into their day, following long-held protocols for depression treatment called “behavior activation.” “There is a special kind of trust that can develop when someone feels that the person sitting across from them understands something about their life and their community — someone who has walked the same path,” Sona Dimidjian, a University of Colorado clinical psychologist who helped found the program, said in an email. “A peer can often say, in effect, ‘I have been there too, and I know how hard it can be.’ That shared experience can also help reduce the stigma and shame that many women feel about depression during pregnancy or the postpartum period.” The concept was based on research from India that found “lay counselors” were effective at reducing mental health symptoms. With the US in a permanent mental health provider shortage, being able to tap into the general population to support new moms was an appealing idea. And evaluations of the program found that it significantly reduced symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress among the Spanish-speaking Latina women who were its initial focus. The biggest endorsement of a peer-support approach like Alma or the peer coaches in FamilyWell Health’s coordinated care program is its target audience. A nationwide survey of new and expecting Latina mothers in the US found that the vast majority thought talking to a peer would make them feel less isolated and more understood compared to a mental health professional. And providers and policymakers around the United States have started taking notice: English and Spanish-language versions of the Alma program are now being implemented in California and New Jersey. There is no panacea for postpartum depression. As Amritha Bhat, who has worked on the MOMCare program at the University of Washington, explained it to me: “Having a multipronged approach is a good way to ensure that treatment reaches those most in need.” The vital importance of a new pill for postpartum depression There are big-picture institutional-level changes that need to be made. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, or DSM, the bible of American psychiatry, currently does not categorize postpartum depression as its own distinct diagnosis. As NPR reported , primary care doctors and pediatricians often do not receive sufficient training to help them recognize the signs of postpartum depression and provide patients with the support they need. There is never enough funding for research or for programs for maternal mental health: The Maternal Mental Health Alliance has been pushing Congress to add millions of dollars in funding for the federal programs that focus on new moms. Peer coaching has not traditionally been covered by health insurance; figuring out how to pay for programs like this is another system-level challenge. But connecting moms to other moms can help the people who need support right now. Sometimes that can happen through organized programs like Alma or FamilyWell; the experts working on those initiatives want to make them an integrated part of post-delivery medical care. But that support might also be found informally in a new parent’s everyday life. There are a lot of social media and in-person groups for new moms to get together, sometimes at a local library or other community organization. Gaulton leaned on a friend when she was struggling after her own pregnancy. As Gaulton emphasized to me, most cases of postpartum depression never escalate into a tragedy. This is a scary condition — but it’s treatable. “I just want laypeople to know that the typical case is someone like me who had some symptoms of depression, anxiety,” she said. “I found help. I got better.” See More : Health Health Care Policy Public Health A federal judge just discovered a whole new way to place ICE above the law Take a mental break with the newest Vox crossword One of the Supreme Court’s worst ideas could save the midterms from Trump The Supreme Court just gave Trump his illegal ballroom What would it take to actually stop the data centers? 健康  
我们其实知道如何帮助患有产后抑郁症的母亲  
Lindsay Clancy的审判揭示了我们在产后抑郁症上的失败。以下是改善之道。  
作者：Dylan Scott  
2026年9月1日，晚上9:10 UTC  
一波地方项目正在提供关于如何更好地提供产后抑郁症护理的有前景的新思路。  
Getty Images  
Dylan Scott为Vox报道健康话题，引导读者了解改善健康过程中出现的新机遇与挑战。他在加入Vox之前，已有超过10年的健康政策报道经验，曾为《治理》杂志、Talking Points Memo和STAT撰稿，2017年加入Vox。  
作为公共服务，我们向所有读者开放这篇报道。今天就成为会员，支持我们的新闻事业。  
Lindsay Clancy的审判——这位马萨诸塞州母亲被指控杀害她的三个孩子——充满了痛苦的假设：如果她有更多支持会怎样？如果她有更多可以倾诉的人会怎样？所有这些痛苦是否可以避免？无论这个特定案件的结果如何，这些都是紧迫的问题，因为数百万女性经历过产后抑郁症。严重的产后精神病可能极为罕见，但每年在美国分娩的女性中，至少有八分之一会经历一些抑郁症状——而且这个数字可能被低估了。  
陪审团最终将决定是否判定她因孩子的死亡而有罪；到周二早上，陪审员仍无法达成一致裁决，但案件法官命令他们继续审议。他们的裁决部分将取决于他们是否相信Clancy在杀害孩子时神志清醒——辩方不否认基本事实——还是如她的律师所主张的那样，她在经历严重的精神病，应因此不对自己的行为负责。  
Clancy的案件已成为全国孕产妇心理健康的焦点——一场引人入胜的法庭剧，同时揭示了新妈妈的心理健康多年来如何被医疗系统和研究界忽视。面对这样的悲剧，很容易感到绝望，而许多报道——正确地——聚焦于它所暴露的系统在为女性提供所需护理方面的缺口。但即使现在，我们仍有理由感到乐观。  
美国各地的医生和医疗工作者正在试验可以改善产后心理护理的策略。他们发现了一个可以在新妈妈挣扎时提供帮助的秘密成分：其他经历过同样事情的妈妈们。  
“你刚生了孩子。你对一个新的人类生命负责。要兼顾生活中的一切真的很难，”Jessica Gaulton博士说，她是儿科医生，创立了FamilyWell Health，一个产后心理健康支持服务。

该计划将同伴教练纳入其中，他告诉我。“女性常常需要的只是有人在身边支持她们。”产后抑郁症是一个医疗系统问题，一个公共健康问题——但它也是一个极其个人化的问题。帮助人们建立联系，让她们不再感到孤单，是我们改善美国母亲产后状况的一种方式。而一波本地项目——以及表明这些项目确实有效的研究——正在提供一些有前景的新思路，帮助我们为产后抑郁症提供更富有同情心和更有效的护理。在克兰西试验期间，孕产妇心理健康联盟列出了五项可以采取的步骤，以改善产后护理。其中首要任务之一是改善不同医疗服务提供者之间的护理协调，这些提供者会在新妈妈分娩后为她提供看诊。所谓的“协作护理模式”多年来一直在蓄势发展，自十多年前在西雅图金县首次用于医疗补助患者的产后护理以来，该模式已扩展到其他地区，但基本原则是：照顾新妈妈并关注她的心理健康需要一个完整的团队，并且需要一个关键人物来帮助管理她们的护理。例如，在洛杉矶，一个非营利组织团体正在结束基于协作护理模式的五年试点项目，新妈妈会被分配一名行为健康护理经理。该经理负责进行评估和简短干预，与精神科顾问合作持续评估患者的状况，并与产科/妇科医生或初级保健医生合作管理患者的治疗。与其等精神科医生有空位时才去看诊，当新妈妈当下正在挣扎时，她现有的医疗服务提供者可以在心理健康专业人士的支持下介入，管理产后抑郁症状。电子邮件（必填）注册提交您的电子邮件即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用谷歌隐私政策和服务条款。在评估中，该模式在减轻症状方面一直优于其他标准护理。但是，尽管我们已经开始看到协作护理模式在美国其他地区推广，但由于各种后勤和财务原因，其进展一直断断续续。孕产妇心理健康联盟正在敦促医疗系统和保险公司投资于更多护理协调项目。现在，一些服务提供者正在协作护理模式的基础上增加一个重要新元素：同伴支持。在华盛顿，MOMCare项目正在试验同伴“导航员”，帮助患者找到合适的护理地点。

他们所需要的。在马萨诸塞州，Gaulton的FamilyWell Health与妇产科诊所合作提供心理健康服务，启动了一个试点项目，增加了经过认证的行为健康教练。这些人员之所以被招募，是因为她们自身有分娩和产后抑郁症状的经历；教练通常是导乐、护士和助产士。患者每周与教练交谈一到两次，设定目标并获得积极反馈，而教练则有一套协议，在发现患者需要更严重支持时遵循。4月发布的一项研究发现，这种新的教练驱动方法成功减轻了抑郁和焦虑症状。患者通过同伴教练平均在9天内缓解抑郁症状，而通过持牌治疗师则需要8天。换句话说，被分配到同伴组的母亲恢复速度几乎与接受专业治疗的母亲一样快。Gaulton表示，她之所以将同伴教练概念引入FamilyWell Health，是因为她自己作为新手妈妈的经验。她难以识别自己的抑郁症状。当她意识到时，她依靠了在工作医院的一位朋友兼新生儿科同事的帮助。然后在新冠期间，她看到母亲们带着原本健康的婴儿在那场改变世界的公共卫生紧急事件中挣扎。“我意识到我们未能充分利用教练，”Gaulton说。“几十年来，我们一直在这个领域使用同伴群体、同伴教练来提供支持，但从未正式化。没有正式培训。”因此，她决定创立一家新公司，专门支持新手妈妈的心理健康——并将这些经验带了过去。这一理念——培训有经验的妈妈帮助新手妈妈——在全国范围内正逐渐获得关注。在科罗拉多州，科罗拉多大学的研究人员启动了一个名为Alma的项目，该项目将新手妈妈与另一位经历过相同经历并接受过专门培训以提供情感支持的女性联系起来。该项目的导师接受80小时的培训，然后与新手妈妈进行多达10次的面对面或虚拟会面，讨论什么让她们感觉良好，以及如何将其融入日常生活，遵循长期以来的抑郁治疗协议，称为“行为激活”。“当一个人觉得坐在对面的人理解她们的生活和社区中的某些事情——一个走过同样道路的人时，一种特殊的信任就会发展起来，”帮助创立该项目的科罗拉多大学临床心理学家Sona Dimidjian在一封电子邮件中说。“同伴通常可以说，实际上，‘我也经历过，我知道这有多难。’那种分享”

亲身经历也有助于减少许多女性在孕期或产后对抑郁所感到的污名和羞耻感。”这一理念基于印度的一项研究，该研究发现“非专业辅导员”在减轻心理健康症状方面效果显著。鉴于美国长期存在心理健康服务提供者短缺的问题，利用普通人群来支持新手妈妈是一个颇具吸引力的想法。项目评估显示，该计划显著减轻了以西班牙语为母语的拉丁裔女性（最初的重点对象）的抑郁、焦虑和压力症状。像Alma或FamilyWell Health协调护理项目中的同伴教练这类同伴支持方法，最大的认可来自其目标受众。一项针对美国新手和待产拉丁裔母亲的全国性调查发现，绝大多数人认为，与心理健康专业人士相比，与同伴交谈会让她们感到更少的孤立感和更多的理解。美国各地的服务提供者和政策制定者已开始关注：Alma项目的英语和西班牙语版本现已在加利福尼亚州和新泽西州实施。产后抑郁没有万能药。正如华盛顿大学MOMCare项目的研究者Amritha Bhat向我解释的那样：“采取多管齐下的方法是确保治疗惠及最需要人群的好途径。”产后抑郁新药至关重要，但还需要宏观的机构层面变革。美国精神病学“圣经”《精神障碍诊断与统计手册》（DSM）目前并未将产后抑郁列为独立诊断类别。据NPR报道，初级保健医生和儿科医生往往未接受足够培训，以识别产后抑郁的迹象并为患者提供所需支持。孕产妇心理健康的研究和项目资金永远不足：孕产妇心理健康联盟一直在推动国会为专注于新手妈妈的联邦项目增加数百万美元资金。同伴辅导传统上不在健康保险覆盖范围内；如何为这类项目买单是另一个系统层面的挑战。但将妈妈们联系起来，可以帮助那些现在就需要支持的人。有时这可以通过像Alma或FamilyWell这样的组织项目实现；这些项目的专家希望将其整合到产后医疗护理中。但这种支持也可能在新手父母的日常生活中非正式地找到。许多社交媒体和线下团体为新手妈妈提供聚会机会，有时在本地图书馆或其他社区场所。

##段落
戈顿在自己产后挣扎时依靠了一位朋友。正如戈顿向我强调的，大多数产后抑郁症案例从未升级为悲剧。这是一种令人恐惧的状况——但它是可以治疗的。“我只想让普通人知道，典型病例是像我这样有一些抑郁、焦虑症状的人，”她说。“我找到了帮助。我好转了。”查看更多：健康 医疗保健政策 公共卫生 一位联邦法官刚刚发现了一种全新的方式，将ICE置于法律之上 用最新的Vox填字游戏来放松一下脑筋 最高法院最糟糕的想法之一可能在中期选举中拯救特朗普 最高法院刚刚给了特朗普他的非法舞厅 真正阻止数据中心需要什么？电子邮件（必填）注册 提交您的电子邮件即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用Google隐私政策和服务条款。广告商内容 来自 这是原生广告的标题

readings.title: The perks and pitfalls of laughing at yourself
body: 3 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Laurie Clarke Researchers are finally beginning to understand the real impacts of poking fun at ourselves – and how to avoid the pitfalls. Why do some schoolchildren become outcasts? In the 1990s, psychologists set out to investigate why some kids were excluded by their peers. They discovered two archetypes. Some of the rejected children were bullying and aggressive. Others were meek and subservient. Both shared one quality: an inability to take a joke .  The first group responded to teasing with anger or violence, while the second felt wounded and withdrew. Both interpreted the intended humour as an insult, something that couldn't possibly be in good faith. More socially assured kids, on the other hand, shrugged off teasing, or were amused by it. Whether we can laugh at ourselves can clearly have consequences from an early age.  Studies show that throughout life, a more light-hearted and humorous outlook on life is better for your mental health, relationships and overall prospects. Still, opinion on whether it is a good idea to laugh at yourself specifically has long been divided. Now, though, researchers are finally beginning to understand the nuance of what it really means to poke fun at ourselves – and when and how it might be beneficial. Is it even possible to laugh at yourself? Plato didn't think so. The Ancient Greek philosopher believed that humour was triggered by feeling superior to others – particularly those who delusionally believe they are better-looking or wiser than they really are. If you really hate people laughing at you, you could be a gelotophobe – someone with an acute sensitivity to laughter More than 1,000 years later, in 1651, English philosopher Thomas Hobbes largely agreed . The exception – when people were occasionally able to laugh at themselves – was when reflecting on a past foolishness, which demonstrated how much worldlier they had become in the interim. Eventually, philosophers began to allow that not all humour was motivated by spite. In the 18th Century, for example, the popular "incongruity theory" proposed that hilarity often results from an unexpected violation of social norms. Still, whether people can actually laugh at themselves remained a contentious topic right up until recent times. Most humour research from the past 50 years has relied on asking people if they can laugh at themselves and taking their word for it. But like the weekly units of alcohol people confess to on doctors' forms, there was a possibility that the reports were a little aspirational. Perhaps people weren't quite as sporting as they claimed. In 2011, though, European researchers tested the ability using an experimental set-up instead. They invited test subjects into the lab and covertly videotaped their faces. When they next came in, the subjects were presented with distorted, fun-house mirror style images of their faces, and their reactions were recorded. Not everyone was amused, but 80% at least smiled when unexpectedly encountering the image. Forty per cent were extra tickled and laughed aloud. "Now the science is quite settled that yes, it is possible to laugh at oneself, and there are actually quite numerous benefits associated with that," says Sonja Heintz, a lecturer in psychology at Plymouth University, UK, who researches humour. Being able to laugh at yourself is one of the most challenging types of humour to master, claimed influential American humour researcher Paul McGhee in 2010. In McGhee's seven-step humour programme (targeted at those suffering "terminal seriousness" like Plato), learning to laugh at oneself was the penultimate step – second only in difficulty to "finding humour in stressful situations."  McGhee saw laughing at yourself as the gateway to other types of humour; a "core component" of a more mirthful existence. "Because if someone takes themselves very seriously, it's difficult to engage in humour in general," explains Heintz.   Some find self-mockery easier to master than others. If you really hate people laughing at you, you could be a gelotophobe – someone with an acute sensitivity to laughter. "You might be sitting in a cafe and joking with your friends, and someone might approach you and ask, why did you laugh at me?" says René Proyer, psychology professor at Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg in Germany. For gelotophobes, even a smile can indicate their interlocutor thinks them a ridiculous person.  There is no one factor explaining why one might become a gelotophobe, but Proyer says that a very strict and punishing style of parenting is one risk factor . Another is an early traumatic experience of having been laughed at. "So a really embarrassing situation at school, for example," says Proyer, "where you are the butt of jokes for weeks, months, perhaps years." Autism appears to be another risk factor . There also seems to be a cultural dimension. East Asian countries generally have higher levels of gelotophobia than Western nations, something researchers attribute to those belonging to collectivistic cultures being less likely to single themselves out for attention, or to engage in humour as a coping mechanism. These cultures tend to believe humour is best left to the professionals. In China, for example, people are more likely to associate humour with "experts", i.e. comedians, than everyday citizens. Like the children unable to take teasing, gelotophobes tend to experience worse psychological and interpersonal outcomes. The trait has been tied to lower life satisfaction, greater friendship avoidance, and increased loneliness and depression. The opposite trait is gelotophilia, the joy of being laughed at by others, which has been linked to stronger social connectedness. One way this can manifest is in "playfulness", the tendency to take oneself and the world lightly. "Playful people are able to frame or reframe everyday situations in a way such that they experience them as entertaining or intellectually stimulating or personally interesting," says Proyer. "A highly playful person is able to do a boring task or chore and reframe it in a way that is somewhat amusing." Research has established playfulness as a predictor of higher self-esteem and relationship satisfaction .  Most experts agree that humour is beneficial to our relationships. But the kind of humour matters too.  In 2003, Canadian researchers developed the Humor Styles Questionnaire , which divides people's dominant humour type into four categories: affiliative humour, self-enhancing humour, aggressive humour and self-defeating humour.  The questionnaire soon became hugely influential. "It was the first time anyone had considered that humour could be adaptive but also maladaptive," says Claire Fox, professor of psychology of education at the University of Bristol, UK.  Self-enhancing humourists are attuned to the fragile absurdities of humanity and existence. They agree with statements like: "If I am feeling upset or unhappy I usually try to think of something funny about the situation to make myself feel better". These individuals make light of their problems as a coping mechanism. This was seen as an adaptive humour type. "Self-defeating" humour, on the other hand, was thought to be maladaptive. Self-defeating humourists agree with statements like: "I often try to make people like or accept me more by saying something funny about my own weaknesses, blunders, or faults." At the time, this type of humour was seen as signalling neediness and low self-esteem. When Heintz first began researching humour in the 2010s, she was taken aback to find that poking fun at oneself was viewed so negatively by the field. "Because my personal humour style is [that] I make fun of myself all the time," she says. "I don't take myself seriously." Reading the literature, Heintz was surprised to find that someone like her was supposedly at higher risk of anxiety, depression and suicidal ideation. To find out if self-defeatists really were all that self-loathing, Heintz rounded up a group of them and compared them to those with other humour styles. If the predominant thinking was correct, "these people should really suffer with mental health issues", says Heintz. But not a single one did. On the contrary, she found that self-defeating humour was associated with higher levels of self-esteem and better interpersonal relationships. "They all said, 'Well, I struggle a bit with self-esteem. I'm a bit insecure. But making fun of myself is actually a really good way for me to cope with these difficulties, and it gives me a way to connect with others'," says Heintz. Most research finding a connection between self-defeating humour and worse mental health and relationship outcomes is correlational , says Heintz, rather than showing a causal effect. Other research has found that the impacts of self-defeating humour can vary across different contexts. A 2014 study by Fox found that schoolchildren who were the victim of bullying used more self-defeating humour than others, and that this preference became more pronounced over time.  But a follow-up study she carried out in 2016 added nuance to the picture. This study labelled kids based on the type of humour they preferred. One group, dubbed the "self-defeaters", engaged only in self-defeating humour. This group seemed to fare worst, ranking the lowest for self-esteem and becoming lonelier over time. But some kids used self-defeating humour even more than the self-defeatists and didn't suffer the same ill effects. The difference was that these kids, dubbed "humour endorsers", engaged in all four different humour types. While those who solely relied on self-defeating humour suffered a social penalty, the humour endorsers did not.  "This suggested that it's actually okay to use self-defeating humour, as long as you're using it in combination with other styles of humour as well," says Fox.  It's not that self-defeating humour never poses an issue. "If you make fun of yourself and it comes from a place of bitterness and self-hatred, then yes, it's probably not good for you," says Heintz. But Heintz now believes that a lot of the negative press around self-defeating humour might  stem from a methodological issue with the Humor Styles Questionnaire. The questions relating to self-defeating humour often introduce a value judgement, she notes, specifying things like: "I do it too much. I do it more than I should."  Could this negative self-judgement be skewing the results? Heintz is now working on a forthcoming paper evaluating 25 years of the questionnaire where she'll propose a rethink of the self-defeating scale. Other researchers are already devising new scales which distinguish between truly self-defeating humour and its more adaptive varieties (like that old British standby, self-deprecating humour). As good comedians know, you should only mock yourself if you've made peace with the flaw or mistake you're making fun of. If you're making a joke from a place of discomfort, people pick up on that and feel awkward, says Heintz. "We need to know that when people make a joke, it's not to be taken seriously. That safety needs to be there for someone to respond to that humour." Moderation is also something to keep in mind. Between self-deprecating and self-defeating humour, "the distinction appears to be about excess and going overboard", says Fox.  Still, it's clear that learning to laugh at yourself can afford psychological and social benefits. Not taking yourself too seriously has been found to help with coping with life's setbacks. Part of this is the simple reason that if you make a mistake, as everyone does from time to time, you're opting for a positive emotional response (laughter) over a negative one (anger or gloom).  "It's related to self-transcendence, which means that when something goes wrong, we can keep that distance from the event and see it a bit more objectively… see the lighter side of things," says Heintz. "We also know that there is a causal effect between things like life satisfaction , coping skills and general well-being." On the interpersonal side, laughing at yourself can be an important tool in your social arsenal. "It's a very safe way to engage in humour in new situations, if you are with strangers and don't quite know their sense of humour yet," says Heintz. When there is a power differential, it can be especially expedient. Another study by Fox found that lecturers engaging in so-called self-defeating humour were seen more positively by students. And those who laugh off minor errors – as long as they do not impact others – are seen as warmer and more competent .    humour So, if you're one of the terminally serious, how can you go about cultivating a lighter attitude towards yourself? McGhee advocated zeroing in on your sore spots – whether it's your height, weight, baldness or clumsiness – and confronting these "no-laugh zones" head-on. However excruciating at first, he promised "a sense of exhilaration and liberation" will follow "as you become comfortable with joking about the things that used to simply annoy or embarrass you."  The first step is admitting to the things you don't like about yourself to others, starting with the most minor. Then start making jokes. "Let's say you're not very interested in fashion, you could poke fun at, 'Oh, I'm wearing the same old jeans again'," says Heintz. "Or, look, I did my shopping at Temu." Eventually, you're ready to make gags about your most agonising insecurities. More like this •  Why performing stand-up is good for your health •  Why do we laugh inappropriately? •  How I changed my personality in six weeks If prodding at your sore spots feels like too much, you could start by cultivating a more amused attitude in general. Proyer carried out a study where he tested whether it was possible to increase playfulness in participants using simple activities over the course of a week. For example, setting aside 10 minutes each evening to write down the three most playful things that happened during the day, "whether this was a thought that you had, or something you observed on your way to work", says Proyer. By and large, the participants perceived themselves as more playful up to three months afterwards – as well as reporting reduced levels of depressiveness and greater happiness.  So what was the most playful thing that happened to you today? Write it down and laugh yourself silly. --  For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.  For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram .  Psychology Mental health Wellbeing Health Comedy Features

3天前 分享 保存 设为Google偏好 Laurie Clarke 研究人员终于开始理解自嘲的真正影响——以及如何避免其中的陷阱。为什么有些学童会成为被排斥的对象？在1990年代，心理学家着手调查为什么有些孩子被同龄人排挤。他们发现了两种典型类型。一些被排斥的孩子表现出欺凌和攻击性，而另一些则温顺和服从。两者共有一个特质：无法接受玩笑。第一组对戏弄的反应是愤怒或暴力，而第二组则感到受伤并退缩。两者都将本意幽默解读为侮辱，认为其不可能出于善意。相比之下，更具社交自信的孩子能对戏弄一笑置之，或觉得有趣。我们是否能自嘲，显然从幼年时期就可能产生影响。研究表明，在整个生命过程中，对生活抱持更轻松幽默的态度，对心理健康、人际关系和整体前景都更有益。尽管如此，关于自嘲是否明智，长期以来意见分歧。不过，现在研究人员终于开始理解自嘲真正含义的微妙之处——以及它何时、如何可能有益。自嘲是否甚至可能实现？柏拉图不这么认为。这位古希腊哲学家相信，幽默源于感觉自己优于他人——尤其是那些妄想自己比实际更漂亮或更聪明的人。如果你真的讨厌别人嘲笑你，你可能是一个“笑惧症”患者——对笑声极度敏感的人。一千多年后，在1651年，英国哲学家托马斯·霍布斯大体同意这一观点。例外情况——当人们偶尔能自嘲时——是在反思过去的愚蠢行为时，这展示了他们在期间变得多么世故。最终，哲学家们开始承认并非所有幽默都出于恶意。例如，在18世纪，流行的“不协调理论”提出，欢闹往往源于对社会规范的意外违反。尽管如此，人们是否真的能自嘲，直到最近仍是一个争议性话题。过去50年的大部分幽默研究依赖于询问人们是否能自嘲，并相信他们的说法。但就像人们在医生表格上承认的每周酒精单位一样，这些报告可能有点过于理想化。也许人们并不像他们声称的那样大度。然而，在2011年，欧洲研究人员改用实验设置来测试这种能力。他们邀请测试对象进入实验室，并秘密地……

他们录下了自己的面部表情。下次来访时，受试者面对的是哈哈镜式的扭曲面部图像，并记录下他们的反应。并非所有人都觉得有趣，但80%的人在意外看到图像时至少会微笑，40%的人格外被逗乐，放声大笑。“如今科学已相当确定：是的，人能够自嘲，而且这确实带来许多好处，”英国普利茅斯大学心理学讲师、研究幽默的索尼娅·海因茨说。美国有影响力的幽默研究者保罗·麦吉在2010年声称，能够自嘲是最难掌握的幽默类型之一。在麦吉的七步幽默计划（针对像柏拉图那样“极度严肃”的人）中，学会自嘲是倒数第二步——难度仅次于“在压力情境中寻找幽默”。麦吉将自嘲视为通往其他幽默类型的门户，是更快乐生活的“核心组成部分”。“因为如果一个人过于严肃对待自己，整体上就很难投入幽默，”海因茨解释道。

有些人比其他人更容易掌握自嘲。如果你真的讨厌别人笑你，你可能是一个“被笑恐惧症”患者——对笑声极度敏感。“你可能坐在咖啡馆和朋友开玩笑，有人走近你问，你为什么笑我？”德国哈勒-维滕贝格马丁·路德大学心理学教授雷内·普罗耶说。对被笑恐惧症患者而言，即使一个微笑也可能表明对方认为他们可笑。没有单一因素能解释为何一个人会成为被笑恐惧症患者，但普罗耶表示，非常严格且惩罚性的教养方式是风险因素之一，另一个因素是早年被人嘲笑的创伤经历。“例如，在学校遇到非常尴尬的情况，”普罗耶说，“你成为笑话的对象，持续数周、数月甚至数年。”自闭症似乎是另一个风险因素，似乎也存在文化维度。东亚国家通常比西方国家有更高水平的被笑恐惧症，研究人员将此归因于集体主义文化中的人不太可能自我突出以吸引注意，或不太可能将幽默作为应对机制。这些文化往往认为幽默最好留给专业人士。例如，在中国，人们更可能将幽默与“专家”（即喜剧演员）而非普通公民联系起来。就像无法忍受戏弄的孩子一样，被笑恐惧症患者往往经历更差的心理和人际关系结果。这一特质与较低的生活满意度、更少的友谊

##段落

回避、孤独感和抑郁情绪的增加。相反的特质是“被笑愉悦”（gelotophilia），即享受被他人取笑的乐趣，这与更强的社会连接感相关。这种特质的一种表现方式是“玩趣性”（playfulness），即以轻松的态度看待自己和世界。“爱玩的人能够以某种方式框定或重新框定日常情境，使它们变得有趣、激发智力或引人入胜，”普罗耶说。“高度爱玩的人能把无聊的任务或琐事重新框定，使之变得有些滑稽。”研究已证实，玩趣性是更高自尊和关系满意度的预测指标。大多数专家同意，幽默对我们的人际关系有益，但幽默的类型也很重要。2003年，加拿大研究人员开发了“幽默风格问卷”，将人们的主导幽默类型分为四类：亲和型幽默、自我提升型幽默、攻击型幽默和自我贬低型幽默。该问卷迅速产生了巨大影响。“这是首次有人考虑到幽默既可以是适应性的，也可能是适应不良的，”英国布里斯托大学教育心理学教授克莱尔·福克斯说。自我提升型幽默者善于捕捉人性和存在中脆弱的荒诞之处。他们认同这样的说法：“如果我感到心烦或不快乐，我通常会试着想些有趣的事来让自己好受些。”这类人将问题轻描淡写，作为应对机制，这被视为一种适应性幽默类型。而“自我贬低型”幽默则被认为是适应不良的。自我贬低型幽默者认同这样的说法：“我常试着通过拿自己的弱点、失误或缺点开玩笑，来让别人更喜欢或接纳我。”当时，这种幽默类型被视为需求感强和低自尊的信号。当海因茨在2010年代开始研究幽默时，她惊讶地发现，该领域对自嘲的评价如此负面。“因为我的个人幽默风格就是总是拿自己开玩笑，”她说。“我不把自己太当回事。”阅读文献后，海因茨惊讶地发现，像她这样的人据称有更高的焦虑、抑郁和自杀意念风险。为了弄清自我贬低者是否真的那么自我厌恶，海因茨召集了一组这样的人，并将他们与其他幽默风格的人进行比较。如果主流观点正确，“这些人应该真的饱受心理健康问题困扰，”海因茨说。但结果没有一个人如此。相反，她发现自我贬低型幽默与更高的自尊水平和更好的心理状态相关。

他们的人际关系。“他们都说，‘嗯，我在自尊方面有点挣扎，有点不自信。但自嘲实际上是我应对这些困难的一个好方法，也给了我与他人建立联系的方式，’”海因茨说。海因茨指出，大多数发现自嘲式幽默与较差的心理健康和人际关系结果之间存在关联的研究，都是相关性研究，而非显示因果关系。其他研究发现，自嘲式幽默的影响可能因情境而异。福克斯在2014年的一项研究发现，遭受欺凌的学童比其他人更多使用自嘲式幽默，且这种偏好随时间推移变得更加明显。但她在2016年进行的后续研究为这一图景增添了细微差别。该研究根据孩子们偏好的幽默类型对他们进行分类。一组被称为“自嘲者”，只使用自嘲式幽默。这组人似乎表现最差，自尊排名最低，并随时间推移变得更加孤独。但有些孩子使用自嘲式幽默甚至比“自嘲者”还多，却没有遭受同样的不良影响。区别在于，这些被称为“幽默认可者”的孩子，参与了所有四种不同类型的幽默。虽然那些仅依赖自嘲式幽默的人在社交上受到惩罚，但幽默认可者却没有。“这表明，只要你将自嘲式幽默与其他风格的幽默结合使用，自嘲实际上是可以的，”福克斯说。并非自嘲式幽默从未构成问题。“如果你自嘲，且这种自嘲源于苦涩和自我憎恨，那么是的，这可能对你不利，”海因茨说。但海因茨现在认为，围绕自嘲式幽默的大量负面报道可能源于幽默风格问卷的方法论问题。她指出，与自嘲式幽默相关的问题常常引入价值判断，比如具体说明：“我做得太多了，比我应该做的要多。”这种负面的自我判断是否可能扭曲结果？海因茨目前正在撰写一篇即将发表的论文，评估该问卷25年的使用情况，她将在其中提议重新思考自嘲量表。其他研究人员已经在设计新的量表，以区分真正的自嘲式幽默与其更具适应性的变体（如英国老牌的自贬式幽默）。正如优秀喜剧演员所知，你只应嘲笑自己已经接受或释怀的缺点或错误。海因茨说，如果你在不自在的地方开玩笑，人们会察觉到并感到尴尬。“我们需要知道，当人们开玩笑时，不应被当真。那就是……”

##段落
安全需要在那里，有人才能回应那种幽默。”适度也是需要铭记的一点。福克斯表示，在自嘲和自毁式幽默之间，“区别似乎在于过度和越界”。尽管如此，显然学会自嘲能带来心理和社交上的益处。研究发现，不把自己太当回事有助于应对生活中的挫折。部分原因很简单：如果你犯了错误——每个人都会不时犯错——你选择的是积极的情绪反应（笑），而不是消极的（愤怒或沮丧）。海因茨说：“这与自我超越有关，意味着当事情出错时，我们能保持与事件的距离，更客观地看待它……看到事情轻松的一面。”“我们也知道，生活满意度、应对技能和整体幸福感之间存在因果关系。”在人际交往方面，自嘲可以成为你社交武器库中的重要工具。海因茨说：“在新环境中，如果你和陌生人在一起，还不了解他们的幽默感，自嘲是一种非常安全的参与幽默的方式。”当存在权力差异时，它尤其有效。福克斯的另一项研究发现，使用所谓自毁式幽默的讲师在学生眼中更受欢迎。而那些对轻微错误一笑置之的人——只要不影响他人——被视为更温暖、更有能力。

##段落
幽默 所以，如果你是那种极度严肃的人，如何培养对自己更轻松的态度呢？麦格希主张聚焦你的痛点——无论是身高、体重、秃头还是笨拙——并正面直面这些“禁区”。尽管起初可能痛苦不堪，他承诺“随着你习惯了拿那些曾经只是惹恼或让你尴尬的事情开玩笑，一种兴奋和解放的感觉”会随之而来。第一步是向他人承认你对自己不满意的地方，从最轻微的做起。然后开始开玩笑。海因茨说：“假设你对时尚不太感兴趣，你可以调侃，‘哦，我又穿这条旧牛仔裤了’。”“或者，看，我在Temu上买的东西。”最终，你准备好拿最折磨人的不安全感开玩笑了。更多类似内容 • 为什么表演脱口秀对你的健康有益 • 我们为什么会不合时宜地笑 • 我如何在六周内改变自己的性格 如果戳自己的痛点感觉太难，你可以从总体上培养一种更幽默的态度开始。普罗耶进行了一项研究，测试是否可以通过一周内的简单活动来增加参与者的玩乐性。例如，

例如，每天晚间留出10分钟，写下当天发生的三件最有趣的事情，“无论是你脑海中的一个念头，还是上班路上观察到的事物”，普罗耶尔说。总体而言，参与者在接下来的三个月里自我感觉更加幽默风趣，同时报告称抑郁程度降低，幸福感增强。那么，今天你遇到的最有趣的事情是什么？写下来，尽情大笑吧。——如需获取有关健康与幸福感的权威见解，请订阅资深健康记者梅丽莎·霍根布姆主理的《健康修复》通讯，她还撰写了《更长寿、更健康地生活》和《迈向平静的六步》课程。欲了解更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境与健康故事，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。心理学 心理健康 幸福感 健康 喜剧 专题

readings.title: 'Brutal' toll of war on Dubai's tourist trade
body: 2 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Sameer Hashmi Last year Dubai welcomed 19.59 million international visitors, making it one of the most-visited cities globally, but the US-Israel war with Iran has had a devastating impact on visitor numbers, and local businesses are struggling. On most evenings, Dubai's restaurants would usually be packed, with the constant buzz of diners, of tourists and residents filling tables across the city. But over the past month, many of those tables have sat empty. For Natasha Sideris, the shift has been sudden and stark. She opened her first restaurant in Dubai in 2014. Over the past decade, her Tashas hospitality group has grown to 14 outlets across the country, employing more than 1,000 people. But the US-Israel war with Iran is now taking a heavy toll on her business. Sideris says many of her restaurants, which are popular with both residents and expats, have seen revenues fall by more than 50%. But outlets that depend heavily on tourists have been hit much harder, with declines of 70% to 80%. The crisis has forced her to cut salaries by 30% for all staff including herself. "The current situation is brutal," she says. "I had a choice – either fire 30% of my staff or cut salaries to save jobs. I chose the latter for now." Sideris adds that the impact would have been worse if many of her outlets were not located inside community malls and close to residential neighbourhoods, where they still rely on local customers. The current tough reality is playing out across much of Dubai's restaurant sector. One senior executive at a restaurant chain, who asked not to be named, said footfall at its outlets has dropped to just 15-20% of normal, forcing them to place more than half of staff on unpaid leave. "We have no option," he says. "We've already shut down a few outlets temporarily, and the rest are operating with minimal staff." The impact is not limited to restaurants. The entire tourism ecosystem – from hotels and travel agencies, to transport companies and airlines – is feeling the strain. Over the past two decades, Dubai has built itself into one of the world's leading tourism hubs. Last year, the emirate welcomed 19.59 million international visitors, making it one of the most-visited cities globally. But since the war began, that momentum has been sharply disrupted. The wider UAE has come under repeated attacks, with Dubai among the key targets of Iran's military response following US and Israeli strikes. Authorities say more than 2,400 missiles and drones have been launched towards the UAE, targeting airports, ports and civilian areas, including hotels and residential buildings. More than 90% of them were intercepted and destroyed, officials say. But some debris has fallen across parts of Dubai, including major residential areas, hotels and the airport. Images of fragments striking the Fairmont hotel on the upscale Palm Island were circulated widely online. To date, 11 people have been killed and more than 185 injured across the UAE, according to authorities in the country. The conflict, which began on 28 February, has disrupted air travel across the region. In the early weeks, tens of thousands of visitors were stranded before being evacuated on special flights. Thousands of regular, scheduled flights have been cancelled since the conflict began, bringing one of the region's busiest travel hubs to a halt at times. Dubai International Airport – the world's busiest for international passengers – handled 95.2 million travellers last year.  Some operations have since resumed, with flag-carrier Emirates operating a reduced flight schedule while working to restore full network operations. But with tourists leaving and the number of new arrivals collapsing, hotel stays in Dubai have fallen steeply. Occupancy levels across Dubai hotels dropped to between 15% and 20% of the usual level for this time of the year in the weeks following the outbreak of the war, according to Mamoun Hmiden, chief business officer at travel booking firm Wego. Hotels have responded with deep discounts, particularly during the Eid period, in an attempt to attract residents. Some luxury properties on Palm Jumeirah, one of the city's premium hotel hubs, have cut prices by as much as half. "The uncertainty is disrupting everyone at the moment," says Hmiden. Some hospitality chains have temporarily shut down some properties or closed certain sections, citing scheduled renovations – a move typically seen during the quieter summer months. A senior executive at an international hospitality group said occupancy at some properties had fallen to single digits. "It made sense to cut operational costs by shutting down for a few weeks and reviewing the situation later," he says. Even business hotels are under pressure. Dubai, a major hub for conferences and events, has seen organisers cancel or postpone large gatherings in the coming months. Majestic Hotels, which operates around 450 rooms across three properties, says occupancy has dropped to record lows. "We are seeing cancellations beyond April," says Varun Raj, cluster director of sales and marketing. "A lot of events have been cancelled, making it difficult for travellers to plan ahead." The slowdown comes after several years of rapid growth. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Dubai was among the first destinations to reopen to international visitors, allowing its tourism sector to recover faster than many global peers. Since then, it has expanded into a broader and more diversified market – strengthening its position as a luxury destination, while also attracting large numbers of mid-market and price-sensitive travellers from regions such as South Asia, Europe and the former Soviet states. That surge in demand has been matched by a sharp increase in supply. Years of growth have driven expansion not only in hotel capacity, but also in short-term apartment rentals across the city. That additional supply is now under pressure. Data firm AirDNA shared that a little over 226,500 short-term bookings were cancelled across the UAE between February 28 to March 29, the first month since the war began.   The downturn is also being felt by the migrant workforce that form the backbone of Dubai's hospitality industry – from restaurant staff to hotel workers.  As demand weakens, many have seen their hours reduced, or they have been placed on unpaid leave. While the UAE's labour system allows companies to adjust quickly to changing conditions, that flexibility can leave workers exposed to sudden income losses. "It feels like we are back to the Covid-19 period," says a South Asian waiter working at a high-end restaurant. There are fears we could lose our jobs again and be forced to go back home." He and several colleagues have been placed on unpaid leave, with no clarity on when – or if – they will return to work. Some hotels, including five-star properties, have started laying off employees. Rights groups say many migrant workers in the UAE are already financially vulnerable, with some carrying debt linked to recruitment fees. The impact of the war is also being felt across the wider Middle East. Research by Tourism Economics, part of Oxford Economics, suggests that between 23 million and 38 million fewer people could travel to the region this year, depending on how long the conflict continues. Between $34bn (£25bn) and $56bn in visitor spending could be lost. "If the war ends soon, there could be a quick recovery," says Hmiden. "But if it drags on, we have to start questioning the entire summer season." This week – Dubai announced $272.26 million in support for businesses, including tourism, over the next three to six months. Hotels will be allowed to delay sales-related fees and tourism dirham charges – a fee applied to guests staying in the city.  Authorities in Dubai are also working on plans to revive tourism once the conflict subsides, including new campaigns and promotional offers.  "The war is out of our control," says one official. "But we are preparing for when it ends." More like this: • How the Iran war is affecting global travel • How a prolonged Middle East conflict could reshape how we fly • Is Dubai's glossy image under threat? Sideris is hoping that landlords will provide rent relief in the form of deferred payments or reduced payments for the time being to support local businesses. For Sideris, the outlook remains uncertain. She says a recovery is possible from October if the war ends soon. But if the conflict continues, the timeline could shift to next year – bringing the risk of layoffs and outlet closures. "We've got enough cash to see us through a month or two... maximum three, and then past that, what do we do? After that, we will have to take tougher calls. Hopefully not. And this insanity ends soon." -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights. For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . Business War News Features Iran war World of Business

##段落
2026年4月2日 分享 保存 设为谷歌首选 Sameer Hashmi

去年迪拜接待了1959万名国际游客，使其成为全球访问量最大的城市之一，但美国-以色列与伊朗的战争对游客数量造成了毁灭性影响，当地企业正苦苦挣扎。

在大多数夜晚，迪拜的餐厅通常座无虚席，食客和游客的喧闹声充斥着全城的餐桌。但在过去一个月里，许多餐桌一直空着。对Natasha Sideris来说，这种转变来得突然而剧烈。她于2014年在迪拜开了第一家餐厅。过去十年间，她的Tashas餐饮集团已发展到全国14家门店，雇用超过1000名员工。但美国-以色列与伊朗的战争现在正对她的生意造成沉重打击。

Sideris表示，她许多受居民和外籍人士欢迎的餐厅收入下降了超过50%。但严重依赖游客的门店受到的冲击要大得多，降幅达70%至80%。这场危机迫使她将所有员工（包括她自己）的薪资削减30%。她说：“目前的情况很残酷。我面临一个选择——要么解雇30%的员工，要么削减薪资以保住工作。我暂时选择了后者。”Sideris补充说，如果她的许多门店不是位于社区商场内、靠近居民区，影响会更严重，因为这些门店仍依赖本地客户。

当前严峻的现实正在迪拜大部分餐饮行业上演。一家连锁餐厅的高级主管（要求匿名）表示，其门店客流量已降至正常水平的仅15-20%，迫使他们让超过一半的员工无薪休假。他说：“我们别无选择。我们已经暂时关闭了几家门店，其余门店以最少人员运营。”

影响不仅限于餐厅。整个旅游生态系统——从酒店、旅行社到运输公司和航空公司——都感受到了压力。过去二十年间，迪拜已将自己打造成全球领先的旅游枢纽之一。去年，这个酋长国接待了1959万名国际游客，使其成为全球访问量最大的城市之一。但自战争开始以来，这一势头被严重打断。

整个阿联酋遭受了多次攻击，迪拜是美国和以色列打击后伊朗军事回应的主要目标之一。当局表示，超过2400枚导弹和无人机被射向阿联酋，目标是机场、港口和民用区域，包括酒店和住宅建筑。官员称，其中超过90%被拦截并摧毁。但一些碎片已落在迪拜部分地区，包括

主要住宅区、酒店和机场。碎片击中高档棕榈岛费尔蒙酒店的画面在网上广泛传播。据阿联酋当局称，截至目前，该国已有11人死亡，超过185人受伤。这场始于2月28日的冲突，扰乱了整个地区的航空旅行。冲突初期，数万名游客被困，随后通过特别航班撤离。自冲突爆发以来，数千个定期航班被取消，有时使该地区最繁忙的旅行枢纽之一陷入停顿。迪拜国际机场——全球国际旅客吞吐量最繁忙的机场——去年接待了9520万人次旅客。部分运营已恢复，旗舰航空公司阿联酋航空正以缩减的航班计划运营，同时努力恢复全面网络运营。但随着游客离去和新 arrivals 锐减，迪拜的酒店住宿率大幅下滑。据旅行预订公司Wego的首席商务官Mamoun Hmiden称，战争爆发后的几周内，迪拜各酒店的入住率降至往年同期正常水平的15%至20%。酒店纷纷大幅折扣，尤其是在开斋节期间，试图吸引本地居民。朱美拉棕榈岛（该市高端酒店集中地之一）的一些豪华酒店，价格下调了多达一半。Hmiden表示：“当前的不确定性正扰乱所有人。”一些酒店连锁集团以计划中的翻修为由，暂时关闭部分物业或区域——这通常是在夏季淡季才会采取的措施。一家国际酒店集团的高级高管表示，部分物业的入住率已降至个位数。他说：“关闭几周以削减运营成本，之后再评估情况，是合理的做法。”即使是商务酒店也面临压力。迪拜是会议和活动的主要中心，但未来数月的大型集会已被组织者取消或推迟。经营三家物业、共约450间客房的Majestic Hotels表示，入住率已降至历史低点。其销售与市场集群总监Varun Raj说：“我们看到4月之后的取消订单。”“大量活动被取消，让旅行者难以提前规划。”此次放缓发生在多年快速增长之后。在新冠疫情期间，迪拜是最早向国际游客重新开放的目的地之一，使其旅游业比许多全球同行恢复得更快。此后，它扩展为更广泛、更多元化的市场——巩固了其作为奢华目的地的地位，同时

同时也吸引了来自南亚、欧洲和前苏联国家等地区的大量中端市场和价格敏感型游客。需求的激增伴随着供应的急剧增加。多年的增长不仅推动了酒店容量的扩张，也促进了城市内短期公寓租赁的发展。这部分新增供应现在面临压力。数据公司AirDNA透露，在2月28日至3月29日期间，即战争开始后的第一个月内，阿联酋各地有超过22.65万笔短期预订被取消。这种下滑也影响了构成迪拜酒店业支柱的移民劳动力——从餐厅员工到酒店工作人员。随着需求减弱，许多人工作时间减少或被安排无薪休假。尽管阿联酋的劳动制度允许企业快速适应变化，但这种灵活性可能使工人面临突然的收入损失。一位在高档餐厅工作的南亚服务员表示：“感觉我们又回到了新冠疫情时期。我们担心会再次失业，被迫回国。”他和几名同事已被安排无薪休假，不清楚何时或是否能够重返工作岗位。一些酒店，包括五星级酒店，已开始裁员。人权组织称，阿联酋许多移民工人经济上本就脆弱，一些人背负着与招聘费用相关的债务。战争的影响也波及整个中东地区。牛津经济研究院旗下旅游经济公司的研究表明，根据冲突持续的时间，今年前往该地区的游客可能减少2300万至3800万人次，游客支出可能损失340亿至560亿美元。“如果战争很快结束，可能会迅速恢复，”赫米登说，“但如果拖延下去，我们不得不质疑整个夏季旅游季。”本周，迪拜宣布在未来三至六个月内为企业（包括旅游业）提供2.7226亿美元的支持。酒店将被允许推迟支付相关销售费用和旅游迪拉姆费用——这是对入住该市游客征收的费用。迪拜当局也在制定计划，在冲突平息后重振旅游业，包括新活动和促销优惠。“战争是我们无法控制的，”一位官员表示，“但我们正在为结束做准备。”更多相关内容：• 伊朗战争如何影响全球旅行• 中东长期冲突如何重塑飞行方式• 迪拜的光鲜形象是否面临威胁？西德里斯希望房东能通过延期付款或减少付款的方式提供租金减免，以支持当地企业。对于西

deris，前景依然不确定。她表示，如果战争很快结束，从十月份起可能迎来复苏。但如果冲突持续，时间表可能推迟到明年——这带来裁员和门店关闭的风险。“我们的现金足以支撑一两个月……最多三个月，之后我们该怎么办？再往后，我们就得做出更艰难的决定。希望不会如此，希望这场疯狂能尽快结束。” -- 如需获取面向董事会及更广泛领域的全球洞察和专家分析，请订阅《商业世界》通讯，而《必读清单》则提供精心挑选的特写和见解。欲了解更多商业及更广泛资讯，请在领英上关注我们。商业 战争 新闻 专题 伊朗 战争 商业世界

readings.title: The plot to disrupt mail-in voting
body: Today, Explained newsletter The plot to disrupt mail-in voting A new whistleblower report warns that Trump’s mail-in voting requirements could cause chaos in the midterm elections. by Caitlin Dewey Sep 1, 2026, 9:10 PM UTC Gift Mail-in ballots sit waiting to be processed by workers at the county election office in Salt Lake City, Utah on October 29, 2020. George Frey/AFP via Getty Images Caitlin Dewey is a senior writer and editor at Vox, where she helms the Today, Explained newsletter. This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here . It took the US government two years to roll out HealthCare.gov, nine months to pilot a direct tax-filing tool…and just 11 weeks to build a new system for processing Americans’ absentee ballots. Before you cheer this rare instance of bureaucratic efficiency, however, please allow the other shoe to drop: That figure comes from an alarming new whistleblower report that foretells potential chaos in this fall’s midterm elections. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. According to the whistleblower, the US Postal Service has rushed out a janky, error-prone processing system in its mad dash to comply with President Donald Trump’s executive order on mail-in ballots . That order, currently paused, would require states to comply with new rules for preparing, tracking, and mailing ballots. Several states have since sued to stop it. If the order does go into effect, however, the Postal Service has to be prepared. So the agency scrambled to hack together its new system — forgoing standard testing procedures and adding requirements that are likely to hold up thousands of outbound ballots, the whistleblower says. According to the report, multiple USPS officials have described the system as “a shit show” that, as of late August, was apt to “completely crash.” “Move fast and break things” is actually not a great look for governments. But the issue goes far beyond one IT meltdown at the post office, or even many IT meltdowns at many post offices. As my colleague Ian Millhiser has covered in depth, Trump’s March executive order could effectively end mail-in voting in several states by imposing a slate of last-minute requirements that election officials don’t have time to implement. Let’s just take the narrow issue of ballot envelopes. Trump’s executive order directed the post office to issue new rules about the design of those envelopes, which the post office did…on August 21. The new rules required that ballot envelopes bear a unique barcode and a logo that the Trump administration claimed would “facilitate proper handling” of election mail. But by that point in the season, a number of states were already preparing to mail their midterm ballots. North Carolina starts mailing general election ballots this week, for instance. More than a dozen other states post theirs by late September. And even in the unlikely case that these states could design, order and distribute millions of compliant envelopes in the next few weeks…it’s not clear the post office could process them. Under the new system, the Postal Service must individually scan every outbound ballot as it heads to voters, a process that the Trump administration says will take “less than a minute” each. Across millions of ballots, however, “less than a minute” adds up: potentially to more than 380,000 hours, in California’s case . That’s enormously concerning , Ian writes. Should courts allow Trump’s order to go into effect, the states that can’t comply won’t be able to do mail-in voting this year. And there are a number of states — including Oregon, Washington, Hawaii, Colorado, Utah, and California — where the entire election is basically vote-by-mail. ”I think it is more likely than not that SCOTUS does not back Trump’s play here. But you can never rule anything out with this Supreme Court,” Ian said. ➨ Listen to “your true self.” In one social science experiment, researchers found that participants who were asked to make an arbitrary decision based on their “true selves” — as opposed to their “rational” brains — were much happier with their choices in the end. So the next time you face a tough decision or a moment of personal ambiguity , you might also consider asking: “What would my true self do today?” Did you know… that Jennifer Lopez inspired Google’s image search feature ? Former executives have said the company only prioritized the tool after JLo wore her famous green Versace dress to the Grammys in 2000. Today’s trivia: What flower did the Aztecs believe could attract the souls of the dead? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword . Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for Tokyo’s original name. That would be Edo. The city was renamed in 1868 as part of a larger political transformation that turned Japan into a modern global power. ##段落
今日解说通讯稿：破坏邮寄投票的阴谋 一份新的吹哨人报告警告称，特朗普的邮寄投票要求可能导致中期选举陷入混乱。作者：凯特琳·杜威 2026年9月1日，晚上9:10 UTC 礼品 2020年10月29日，犹他州盐湖城县选举办公室，邮寄选票等待工作人员处理。乔治·弗雷/法新社 via Getty Images 凯特琳·杜威是Vox的高级撰稿人和编辑，负责《今日解说》通讯稿。本文发表于《今日解说》，这是一份每日通讯，帮助你理解当天最引人注目的新闻和故事。点击此处订阅。美国政府花了两年时间推出HealthCare.gov，九个月试点直接报税工具……而仅用11周就建成了处理美国人缺席选票的新系统。然而，在你为这种罕见的官僚效率欢呼之前，请允许另一只靴子落下：这个数字来自一份令人震惊的新吹哨人报告，它预示着今年秋季中期选举可能出现的混乱。电子邮件（必填） 注册 提交你的电子邮件即表示你同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用谷歌隐私政策和服务条款。据吹哨人称，美国邮政服务在匆忙遵守总统唐纳德·特朗普关于邮寄投票的行政命令时，仓促推出了一套粗糙且易出错的处理系统。该命令目前已被暂停，要求各州遵守准备、跟踪和邮寄选票的新规则。此后，多个州提起诉讼以阻止该命令。然而，如果该命令确实生效，邮政服务必须做好准备。因此，该机构匆忙拼凑出新系统——吹哨人称，该系统放弃了标准测试程序，并增加了可能扣留数千张外发选票的要求。据报告，多名USPS官员将该系统描述为“一场闹剧”，截至8月底，该系统很可能“彻底崩溃”。“快速行动，打破常规”对政府来说其实并不是一个好形象。但问题远不止邮局的一次IT故障，甚至也不止许多邮局的多次IT故障。正如我的同事伊恩·米利希瑟深入报道的那样，特朗普3月的行政命令可能通过施加一系列最后一刻的要求（选举官员没有时间实施），有效终止多个州的邮寄投票。让我们只看选票信封这个狭窄的问题。特朗普的行政命令指示邮局发布关于这些信封设计的新规则，邮局于8月21日发布了这些规则。新规则要求选票信封带有独特的条形码和特朗普政府声称的标识。

将有助于“妥善处理”选举邮件。但到那个时间点，多个州已在准备邮寄中期选举选票。例如，北卡罗来纳州本周开始邮寄普选选票，另有十多个州在9月底前寄出。即便这些州能在未来几周内设计、订购并分发数百万个合规信封（这种情况不太可能），邮政系统能否处理这些邮件也不明朗。在新系统下，邮政服务必须逐一扫描每封寄往选民的外发选票，特朗普政府称这一过程每次只需“不到一分钟”。然而，对数百万张选票而言，“不到一分钟”累积起来可能超过38万小时，以加州为例。伊恩写道，这令人极为担忧。如果法院允许特朗普的命令生效，无法遵守的州今年将无法进行邮寄投票。包括俄勒冈州、华盛顿州、夏威夷州、科罗拉多州、犹他州和加州在内，多个州的选举基本上完全依赖邮寄投票。“我认为最高法院很可能不会支持特朗普的做法。但在这届最高法院面前，你永远不能排除任何可能性，”伊恩说。

##段落
➨ 倾听“真实的自我”。在一项社会科学实验中，研究人员发现，基于“真实自我”（而非“理性”大脑）做出任意决定的参与者，最终对自己的选择满意度更高。因此，下次面临艰难决定或个人迷茫时，你或许也可以问自己：“今天真实的我会怎么做？”

readings.title: Inside Earth's biggest telescope
body: 5 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Richard Fisher In Chile's Atacama Desert, the biggest telescope ever built is taking shape – and it could radically change our view of the Universe. Over the past 200 years, telescopes have got ever-bigger – which has posed a conundrum about what to call them. Some are named after eminent astronomers. Others after their location. But many get their titles from their sheer size. The astronomer William Herschel set the trend in the 18th Century with his Great Forty-Foot Telescope. And today, there's the Southern African Large Telescope , Spain's Gran Telescopio Canarias , and the Large Binocular Telescope in Arizona, to name a few. But what do you call a telescope that's bigger than large? For the scientists and engineers of the Paranal observatory in Chile's Atacama desert, the answer is simple: a process you might call "nominative magnification". In the 1990s, they needed a title for a particularly whopping telescope, which combined several individual instruments into one virtual mega-mirror. They scratched their heads for a while, and decided to name it the Very Large Telescope (VLT) . Now the same astronomers are going even more superlative, building a facility on a second Chilean mountain that will become Earth's biggest eye on the stars. Its name? Naturally, they're calling it the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) . And they are not kidding about the size: the ELT's dome is 80m tall (260ft), and the mirror inside is 39m wide (128ft). With an outer structure due to be completed in 2027, the organisation behind it – a consortium of 16 member states called the European Southern Observatory (Eso) – hope it will be peering into the cosmos by 2030. It's proven to be an enormous engineering challenge too, requiring tens of thousands of tonnes of concrete and steel, and 798 precisely engineered mirror segments , to be shipped to the top of an uninhabited mountain in the desert. Why build such a massive telescope in such a harsh and remote location? To find out, the BBC visited the ELT site in Chile, and discovered an extremely big telescope poised to make extremely big discoveries. In fact, it might even make the biggest discovery of them all. From a distance, it's difficult to get a handle on the size of the ELT. Approaching its mountaintop perch on Cerro Armazones, it first appears as a dot of silver glistening beneath an empty blue sky. Apart from a few road signs and the occasional industrial mine, there is almost no imprint of human habitation in the Atacama Desert, so nothing to offer a sense of scale. All the construction materials must be transported for hours from the nearest city, piece by piece, and the engineers here work in shifts of eight long days and nights before travelling back to their homes, sometimes hundreds of miles away. Look east and there is only boundless wilderness – from some places, you can see as far as Argentina – and to the west, the Pacific Ocean, topped by a sea of inverted cloud. The Atacama is not a desert of sand, but of rough rock, volcanic peaks, and salt flats. In some locations, rain comes only a few times a century, or not at all. With so little moisture, a visitor finds themselves continually licking their dry lips. Dehydration is a real danger, the altitude makes some nauseous, and the thin, cloudless air means that Earth's nearest star will burn your skin faster than almost anywhere else on the planet . Yet within this unforgiving setting, one of the world's most advanced telescopes is gradually assembling. To appreciate how complicated a project the ELT is, you have to step inside. Within the retractable, rotating dome lies a complex lattice of steel beams and moving parts that will hold the giant mirror in place. After a while, the back of your neck begins to ache because you're so frequently gazing upwards. "It's a cathedral in terms of the size and scale," says Michael Booth, the on-site mechanical engineering lead for the ELT, who is accompanying the BBC on a tour of the site. However, "extremely large" does not mean lumbering, or imprecise. On the contrary, assembling the telescope has required extensive planning and minute accuracy, says Booth. "It's too big and too complicated for us to say, 'I hope it works.' It's not like, 'let's hit this button and see if it makes any big noises,'" he says. To illustrate his point, Booth points at removable, millimetre-wide "shim packs" between the giant beams. These are necessary for tiny structural adjustments as the telescope's massive concrete base shrinks over time. That concrete, when it was laid, needed to be extraordinarily flat, he says, to an accuracy of 1/3,600th of a degree, and to account for the Earth's curvature too. (When they were finished, the engineers used the excess wet concrete to make a basketball court on the mountainside, because it was too far to the nearest city to return it before it hardened.) To gather light that has travelled from distant stars and galaxies, and to account for the atmosphere's blurring effects, astronomers need the telescope to be incredibly stable; the slightest wobble will lead to a fuzzy image. "The thing that makes construction of a telescope like this so hard is that usually the bigger you get, the bigger your tolerances – like how much wiggle room you have. But for us, obviously, the light waves don't get bigger," explains Booth. "And so we have to build to the scale of a large commercial building but with the tolerances you find on an optical bench." It's not a static structure, either. During operation, the entire building will rotate to face in different directions, suspended on high-pressure oil. "We float the whole telescope, so it can move basically frictionlessly," says Booth. "It's like an air hockey table." This puck, however, weighs many thousands of tonnes. The ELT's record-breaking mirror, in the centre of the structure, will be assembled from 798 individual, removable hexagonal segments, delicately polished. But unlike your bathroom mirror, there's no protective glass to shield against scrapes or dents. "That's the hard part," says Booth. "Most of the time if something weighs 10 tonnes you can hit it with a hammer. We can't even scratch the surface of it." The mirror segments, shipped from Europe in containers, are currently stored in a warehouse nearby: But when they are placed inside the structure, they will join to form one big mirror that is 39m (128ft) wide : No operating optical-infrared ground telescope currently has a mirror this huge. By comparison, the ELT's little brother – the Very Large Telescope, around 20 kilometres (12 miles) away – is made up of four telescopes each with mirrors of only 8.2m (27ft) diameter (plus four small 1.8m (6ft) diameter auxiliary telescopes). Each has to work together to combine their light. The ELT mirror's size – and the fact that it can change shape in real-time to account for atmospheric turbulence – will allow astronomers to scrutinise many objects with higher resolution than currently possible. In other words, the mirror is a "bigger bucket to collect light", says Eso astronomer Mariya Lyubenova. There's a limit to the sharpness of the images that the current generation of telescopes can create, even space-based telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), currently orbiting the Sun (which incidentally, has a mirror that's only 6.5m (21ft) wide.) Elyar Sedaghati, an Eso staff astronomer at the Paranal observatory, explains why the ELT offers a step-change for astronomers. "I​magine if you have a car that's coming from very far away at night," he says. "The car has two headlights but when it's really far away you cannot distinguish them. You only see a single light. The closer it gets, at some point, you start to separate the two lights." It's the same with stars, but a giant mirror essentially brings such overlapping starlight closer to Earth, allowing astronomers to distinguish what's in the field of view. Therefore, the ELT promises advances right across astronomy and physics. "It's just so multifaceted. It will really push the boundary and push the needle at every possible astronomical subfield that you can think of," says Sedaghati. So for example, the ELT will follow up on discombobulating discoveries recently made by JWST about the distant, early Universe, by imaging very far, very old galaxies that have never been scrutinised before. "It will be really amazing when the ELT starts, because it has a higher angular resolution compared to the James Webb, so we can combine observations," says Sedaghati. A space telescope alone can show us a lot, but a space telescope and a ground telescope together make for a great team. Closer to home, astronomers hope the ELT will be sensitive enough to help them calculate the ages of our own galaxy's oldest stars. The hope is also to peer closer at the stars revolving around the galactic centre, says Lyubenova, which could reveal deviations from current gravitational theories. And in our own neighbourhood, the telescope will be able to track objects like the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS that passed through our Solar System recently. But the biggest prize of all? It could well be the discovery that would change everything: evidence of life beyond Earth. In the 21st Century, we have entered a new era in the search for aliens. Some observers have called it the " age of alien agnosticism ": a time when a growing number of serious scientists strongly believe a basic form of extraterrestrial life is close to showing itself, but cannot yet prove it – their evidence accumulating piece-by-piece . It was once assumed that the discovery of aliens would involve flying saucers, radio signals or Martian megastructures . But it's more likely that we'll spot a more basic form of life first, revealing itself slowly to telescopes. We've already had signs: a compelling recent example was the apparently organic chemicals detected on the exoplanet K2-18b : a tantalising hint of marine organisms. It could be just the beginning. If you talk to serious astronomers about aliens, most are cautious, burnt by hyperbolic media claims , and slightly ticked off that you're not asking them about more sober activities like cataloguing galaxies. But they don't totally discount the possibility. In a recent survey of astrobiologists, physicists and other scientists, almost 90% agreed that it's likely that basic extraterrestrial life exists in the Universe. The numbers in the survey were lower for complex or intelligent life (around 60%), but they were also far from zero. The cosmos, after all, is a big place. "As an astronomer that works in this field, you have to be very careful," says Sedaghati. He is doubtful of finding intelligent life within the same broad expanse of space and time as us. But something like microbes or algae? That's different. "If you think about the number of stars that are only in our own galaxy and the number of planets around that are around these stars, and the proportion of those planets that are in a zone where you could possibly have life… if you just look at the sheer numbers, the probability that life exists somewhere else in the galaxy it's, for me, extremely high. There must be life out there." The sticking point is: what will count as strong evidence? And that's where the ELT comes in. It's not possible to image an exoplanet and see an alien waving back; it's not even possible to image landmasses. But we can study their habitability in other ways. For example, astronomers can infer whether a planet is rocky or gaseous. To do this, "we observe very tiny deviations in the wobble of a star", explains Lyubenova. This reveals the otherwise invisible nearby planet's gravitational effect, which in turn allows a calculation of its mass. Gas giants tend to have higher mass than rocky planets. Crucially, the ELT will be able to measure the masses of smaller, lower mass worlds than currently possible, she says, significantly expanding the candidates for hosting alien life. Astronomers can also analyse the constituents of exoplanet atmospheres, via the light spectrum of the starlight that occasionally passes through them on its way to Earth. "Each chemical element has its own imprint in the spectrum. It's like a fingerprint," says Lyubenova. So if an alien bacteria or some form of strange algae is belching out organic gases, it could show up. At the moment, it's difficult to study exoplanet atmospheres in the habitable zone of other solar systems, because such worlds are too close to the star. Like when you're dazzled by a car headlight, you can't see who is at the wheel. Claims about biosignatures on K2-18b in 2025 were controversial, because as well as disagreements about whether the detected gases are organic, the planet is also right at the edge of possible habitability. The ELT, however, could explore many more candidate worlds. In short, within as little as a decade, it is here – deep in the Chilean desert – that we may finally gain the evidence that aliens are out there, posing existential questions about our position in the cosmos. The age of alien uncertainty would end: we would finally realise that we are no longer alone. More like this: • The hotel where astronomers live like James Bond spies • The light disturbing a dark zone full of telescopes • The spacewalk that saved Hubble What comes after that is unknown. But already, astronomers have their eye on the next telescopes – which could be even bigger. "We are already thinking about other ways of pushing the boundary," says Sedaghati. For example, there are ideas like building lots of telescopes, kilometres apart, and connecting them to make a mega-telescope. In principle, if the existing Very Large Telescope was connected to a new telescope on another mountain-top via an "optical bridge" it would significantly boost its abilities, says Sedaghati. In the more distant future, people have talked about sending a space telescope beyond our Solar System's most distant planets so that we can use the Sun – and the fact its mass bends distant starlight – as a "gravitational lens". Essentially, the telescope would be the size of the Solar System. "This way you would actually not just image a planet around another star – an Earth-sized planet – but you would even be able to map the surface of it," says Sedaghati. "You would be able to tell more or less, where is oceans, where is land? These ideas are out there but it's just our technology needs to catch up." It begs the question: what do you call these behemoths if "extremely large" is already taken? A couple of decades ago, Eso was already considering whether to build the "Overwhelmingly Large Telescope". But a clue might come from an XKCD cartoon that jokes where they could go next: "oppressively colossal" is one option, or perhaps "mind-numbingly vast". For now though, astronomers wait. They know that by the 2030s, a cathedral to human curiosity will finally be peering into the cosmos. What they don't know yet is what it will find. -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.  For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram . 5天前 分享 保存 设为Google偏好 Richard Fisher 在智利的阿塔卡马沙漠，有史以来最大的望远镜正在成形——它可能彻底改变我们对宇宙的认知。过去200年间，望远镜越造越大，这引发了一个关于如何命名它们的难题。有些以著名天文学家命名，有些以所在地命名，但许多则根据其庞大尺寸得名。18世纪，天文学家威廉·赫歇尔以他的“四十英尺大望远镜”开创了这一趋势。如今，有南非大望远镜、西班牙的加那利大望远镜，以及亚利桑那州的大双筒望远镜等。但你会如何称呼一台比“大”还大的望远镜呢？对于智利阿塔卡马沙漠帕拉纳尔天文台的科学家和工程师而言，答案很简单：一个你可以称之为“名称放大”的过程。在1990年代，他们需要为一台特别巨大的望远镜命名，该望远镜将多个独立仪器组合成一个虚拟的巨型镜面。他们挠头思考了一阵，决定将其命名为“甚大望远镜”（VLT）。现在，这些天文学家正更进一步，在智利的第二座山上建造一座设施，它将成为地球观测星辰的最大之眼。它的名字？自然，他们称其为“极大望远镜”（ELT）。而且他们在尺寸上绝非玩笑：ELT的圆顶高80米（260英尺），内部镜面宽39米（128英尺）。外部结构预计于2027年完工，其背后的组织——由16个成员国组成的欧洲南方天文台（Eso）——希望它能在2030年前凝视宇宙。这已被证明是一项巨大的工程挑战，需要数万吨混凝土和钢材，以及798块精密设计的镜面片段，运往沙漠中一座无人居住的山顶。为何在如此严酷偏远的地点建造如此巨大的望远镜？为了寻找答案，BBC访问了智利的ELT现场，发现了一台即将做出极其重大发现的超大望远镜。事实上，它甚至可能做出其中最重大的发现。从远处看，很难把握ELT的尺寸。接近其在阿玛索内斯山顶的栖息地时，它最初只是空蓝天空下闪烁的银色小点。除了少数路标和偶尔的工业矿场，阿塔卡马沙漠几乎无人居住痕迹，因此无法提供尺度感。所有建筑材料必须从最近城市逐件运输数小时，这里的工程师们轮班工作，连续八天八夜后返回家乡。

是的，有时甚至远在数百英里之外。向东望去，只有无边的荒野——从某些地方，你甚至可以看到阿根廷——而向西，则是太平洋，上方覆盖着一片倒置的云海。阿塔卡马并非沙质沙漠，而是由粗糙的岩石、火山峰和盐沼组成。在某些地区，雨水几个世纪才降临一次，甚至从未有过。由于水分如此稀少，游客会发现自己在不停地舔舐干裂的嘴唇。脱水是实实在在的危险，高海拔使一些人感到恶心，而稀薄无云的空气意味着，地球上最近的恒星——太阳——会比地球上几乎任何其他地方更快地灼伤你的皮肤。然而，在这片严酷的环境中，世界上最先进的望远镜之一正在逐步组装成型。要理解ELT（极大望远镜）项目有多么复杂，你必须走进内部。在可伸缩、旋转的圆顶内，是一个由钢梁和活动部件组成的复杂网格，它将支撑巨大的镜面。过了一会儿，你的后颈开始酸痛，因为你频繁地仰望上方。“就尺寸和规模而言，它是一座大教堂，”ELT现场机械工程负责人迈克尔·布斯说，他正陪同BBC参观现场。然而，“极大”并不意味着笨重或粗糙。相反，布斯表示，组装这台望远镜需要周密的规划和极高的精度。“它太大太复杂了，我们不能说‘我希望它能行’。这不像‘让我们按一下这个按钮，看看它会不会发出大响声’，”他说。为了说明他的观点，布斯指着巨大横梁之间可拆卸的、毫米宽的“垫片组”。这些垫片对于微调结构是必需的，因为望远镜巨大的混凝土基座会随时间收缩。他说，铺设混凝土时，它需要极其平坦，精度要达到1/3600度，并且还要考虑地球的曲率。（完工后，工程师们用多余的湿混凝土在山腰上建了一个篮球场，因为距离最近的城市太远，无法在混凝土硬化前将其运回。）为了收集来自遥远恒星和星系的光，并抵消大气层的模糊效应，天文学家需要望远镜极其稳定；最轻微的晃动都会导致图像模糊。“建造这样一台望远镜之所以如此困难，是因为通常你做得越大，你的公差就越大——比如你有多少活动空间。但对我们来说，显然，光波不会变大，”布斯解释道。“因此，我们必须以大型商业建筑的规模来建造，但精度却要达到光学实验台上的标准。”它也不是一个静态结构。在运行期间，望远镜的镜面会

整栋建筑将悬浮在高压油上，旋转以面向不同方向。“我们让整个望远镜浮起来，这样它就能基本无摩擦地移动，”布斯说，“就像空气曲棍球台一样。”然而，这个“圆盘”重达数千吨。ELT创纪录的镜面位于结构中心，将由798个可拆卸的六边形小镜片精心抛光后组装而成。但与浴室镜子不同，它没有保护玻璃来防止刮擦或凹陷。“这是最难的部分，”布斯说，“大多数时候，如果某物重10吨，你可以用锤子敲它，但我们连碰都不能碰它的表面。”镜片从欧洲用集装箱运来，目前存放在附近的仓库中：但一旦放入结构内部，它们将拼接成一个宽39米（128英尺）的大镜子：目前运行中的光学红外地面望远镜中，没有一面镜子有这么大。相比之下，ELT的“小兄弟”——距离约20公里（12英里）的甚大望远镜——由四架望远镜组成，每架镜面直径仅8.2米（27英尺）（外加四个直径1.8米（6英尺）的小型辅助望远镜），每架都必须协同工作以合并光线。ELT镜面的大小——以及它能实时变形以应对大气湍流的事实——将使天文学家能以比目前更高的分辨率仔细观测许多天体。换句话说，这面镜子是一个“更大的收集光线的桶”，ESO天文学家玛丽亚·柳贝诺娃说。当前一代望远镜（包括像詹姆斯·韦伯太空望远镜（JWST）这样目前在绕太阳运行、镜面宽度仅为6.5米（21英尺）的太空望远镜）所能产生的图像清晰度存在极限。ESO帕拉纳尔天文台的工作人员天文学家埃利亚尔·塞达加蒂解释了ELT为何能为天文学家带来质的飞跃。“想象一下，夜晚有一辆车从很远的地方驶来，”他说，“车有两个前灯，但距离很远时，你无法分辨它们，只能看到一个光点。当车靠近时，在某个时刻，你开始分离这两个光点。”恒星也是如此，但巨大的镜面本质上将这种重叠的星光拉近到地球，让天文学家能分辨视野中的物体。因此，ELT有望在天文学和物理学的各个领域取得进展。“它实在太多元了。它将真正推动边界，推动你能想到的每一个天文学子领域的进步，”塞达加蒂说。例如，ELT将跟进JWST最近关于遥远早期宇宙的令人困惑的发现，通过成像非常遥远、非常

##段落
那些从未被仔细审视过的古老星系。“当ELT开始运行时，那将真的令人惊叹，因为它的角分辨率比詹姆斯·韦伯更高，所以我们可以结合观测，”塞达加提说。单独的太空望远镜能向我们展示很多，但太空望远镜和地面望远镜联手，会组成一个强大的团队。更近一些的地方，天文学家希望ELT的灵敏度足以帮助他们计算我们银河系中最古老恒星的年龄。柳贝诺娃说，还希望能更近距离地观测围绕银河系中心旋转的恒星，这可能揭示当前引力理论的偏差。而在我们的近邻环境中，这台望远镜将能够追踪像最近穿过我们太阳系的星际彗星3I/ATLAS这样的天体。但最大的收获是什么？很可能就是那个会改变一切的发现：地球之外存在生命的证据。在21世纪，我们进入了寻找外星人的新时代。一些观察者称之为“外星不可知论时代”：在这个时代，越来越多严肃的科学家坚信某种基本形式的地外生命即将显现，但还无法证明——他们的证据正在一点一点地积累。曾有人假设，发现外星人会涉及飞碟、无线电信号或火星巨型结构。但更有可能的是，我们会先发现一种更基本的生命形式，它通过望远镜慢慢显露出来。我们已经有了迹象：一个引人注目的近期例子是在系外行星K2-18b上探测到的明显有机化学物质——这是一个关于海洋生物的诱人暗示。这可能只是开始。如果你和严肃的天文学家谈论外星人，大多数人会很谨慎，被媒体夸张的报道烧灼过，并且有点恼火你没有问他们更冷静的活动，比如编目星系。但他们并没有完全排除这种可能性。在最近一项对天体生物学家、物理学家和其他科学家的调查中，近90%的人同意宇宙中很可能存在基本形式的地外生命。对于复杂或智慧生命，调查中的数字较低（约60%），但也远非零。毕竟，宇宙是一个广阔的地方。“作为在这个领域工作的天文学家，你必须非常小心，”塞达加提说。他怀疑在和我们相同广阔的时空范围内能找到智慧生命。但像微生物或藻类那样的东西？那就不同了。“如果你想想仅在我们银河系中恒星的数量，围绕这些恒星的行星数量，以及这些行星中处于可能存在生命区域的比例……如果你只看纯粹的数字，生命存在的概率”

如果银河系其他地方存在生命，对我来说，可能性极高。那里一定有生命存在。”症结在于：什么才算作强有力的证据？这正是ELT发挥作用的地方。我们不可能对系外行星成像并看到外星人挥手致意，甚至不可能成像陆地。但我们可以通过其他方式研究它们的宜居性。例如，天文学家可以推断一颗行星是岩石质还是气态的。为此，“我们观测恒星摆动中非常微小的偏差”，柳贝诺娃解释道。这揭示了原本不可见的邻近行星的引力效应，进而允许计算其质量。气态巨行星往往比岩石行星质量更大。她说，关键在于，ELT将能够测量比目前可能更小、质量更低的世界，从而显著扩大可能孕育外星生命的候选行星范围。天文学家还可以通过偶尔穿过系外行星大气层到达地球的星光光谱，分析其大气成分。“每种化学元素在光谱中都有其独特印记，就像指纹一样，”柳贝诺娃说。因此，如果外星细菌或某种奇异藻类排放出有机气体，就可能显现出来。目前，研究其他太阳系宜居带中的系外行星大气层很困难，因为这些世界离恒星太近。就像被汽车前灯晃到眼睛时，你看不见驾驶座上的人。2025年关于K2-18b上生物特征的说法存在争议，因为除了对检测到的气体是否为有机物存在分歧外，该行星也恰好处于可能宜居的边缘。然而，ELT可以探索更多候选世界。简而言之，在短短十年内，就在智利沙漠深处，我们可能最终获得外星人存在的证据，引发关于我们在宇宙中位置的深刻问题。外星不确定性时代将结束：我们最终会意识到我们不再孤独。更多类似内容：• 天文学家像詹姆斯·邦德间谍一样居住的酒店• 干扰布满望远镜暗区的光线• 拯救哈勃太空望远镜的太空行走。之后会发生什么未知。但天文学家已经将目光投向下一代望远镜——它们可能更大。“我们已经在思考其他突破边界的方法，”塞达加提说。例如，有想法建造许多相距数公里的望远镜，并将它们连接起来组成一个巨型望远镜。塞达加提说，原则上，如果现有的甚大望远镜通过“光学桥”连接到另一座山顶的新望远镜，将显著提升其能力。在更遥远的未来，人们已讨论

关于将一台太空望远镜送往太阳系最遥远行星之外的想法，是为了利用太阳——以及其质量弯曲遥远星光的事实——作为“引力透镜”。本质上，这台望远镜的规模将相当于整个太阳系的大小。“这样，你不仅能够直接成像围绕另一颗恒星的行星——一颗地球大小的行星——甚至还能绘制其表面地图，”塞达加提说。“你大致能分辨出哪里是海洋，哪里是陆地？这些构想已经存在，但关键在于我们的技术还需追赶。”这引出一个问题：如果“极大”已被占用，这些庞然大物又该如何命名？几十年前，欧洲南方天文台已在考虑是否建造“压倒一切望远镜”。但线索或许来自一幅XKCD漫画，它开玩笑地提出下一步可能的命名：“压迫性巨大”是一个选项，或者或许是“令人脑麻木的浩瀚”。不过，目前天文学家们仍在等待。他们知道，到2030年代，一座人类好奇心的“大教堂”终将凝视宇宙。他们尚不知道的是，它将发现什么。——如果你喜欢这个故事，请订阅《基本清单》新闻通讯——精选的特稿、视频及不容错过的新闻，每周两次发送至你的邮箱。欲获取更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境与健康报道，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。天文学望远镜太空宇宙物理学特稿

readings.title: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
body: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> Maria Petrishina / iStock

While there are various approaches to leading a team, many of us land on common questions in the search for an effective leadership style: How can I be there for my team? Do I need to command respect, or earn it? And the most crucial question of all: How can I make sure that my team trusts me?

Cady Coleman has been confronting these questions throughout her career as a chemist, engineer, Air Force colonel and astronaut. In conversation with TED science curator David Biello, Coleman shared three strategies to establish — and maintain — trust in a leader. Whatever your career is, these tips can help you to prepare your team to face any challenge you come across — in outer space or here on Earth.
People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team” … But maybe there should be.
1. Be brave enough to get to know your team members as individuals

People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team”… But maybe there should be, says Coleman. Every member of your team is a whole person, and since so many of the problems we face at work are interdisciplinary, understanding who each individual is beyond the 9-to-5 is valuable. Being vulnerable enough to get to know your team this way is an essential skill for any leader.

When you are able to say, “I think your world is different from mine, and I’d like to understand more about it,” you’re not just building trust; you’re opening a communication channel that teaches you more about your teammate’s qualities, says Coleman. This type of conversation requires the willingness and bravery to be vulnerable. Once you know what everyone brings to the table, you can foster the growth of qualities that can lead the team to collective success.

For example, as Coleman prepared for life on the space station, her advisors warned that the long periods of time away from family might be too much to handle. For her, however, this wasn’t a problem — she had been commuting and working away from her family for more than a decade. After sharing her experience, her colleagues realized she’d not only be adaptable to life on the space station, but also she could help others cope with the change, too.
2. Create a culture that’s open to everyone’s ideas
While leaders have to guide their teams, it’s equally important to let everyone know that they can advocate for themselves and bring their own ideas to the table.

Coleman benefitted from such leadership at NASA when she was training to go to the space station. In the face of budget cuts, NASA announced that they’d be eliminating their smaller space suits, meaning that if someone wasn’t qualified to use a larger space suit, they couldn’t go to the space station. This presented a choice for Coleman: wait for NASA to acquire suits that fit her or figure out how she could train in the larger suits. By working with NASA’s decision makers, Coleman was able to shift her training to use the bigger suits. Had she not felt the freedom to speak up, she says, she would have been waiting 10 years to go to the space station in a small suit.
When you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily.

Sometimes establishing trust in the workplace can be more difficult than you expect, but when you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily. Workplace dynamics are always changing — maybe a teammate’s work/life priorities have shifted, or a big mistake requires you all to work together under new pressures. These challenges make fostering trust tricky, but they are also moments of opportunity.

If a new challenge has arisen or trust has been breached, Coleman reminds us to “always figure out the why and the what.” Make sure to ask: why has this happened, why do they feel this way, and what can be done about it? Be open to different points of view, and don’t give up if you don’t get through at first. Connection is often in the smaller things you do; talk about food or music, write a note to compliment an idea and ask to hear more. This level of connection and vulnerability may not seem intuitive at first, but as you make trust a core part of your mission, it becomes easy.

Trust, Coleman reminds us, is both given and earned. As a woman, she knew gaining the trust of some male colleagues might be extra challenging. Her approach was simple: she performed well and, with patience and persistence, learned her colleagues’ language and taught them hers. The challenges in gaining trust will always be there, but if you model vulnerability, openness and understanding for your team, you’ll find the rewards will always be there, too.

This post was adapted from a recent LinkedIn Live conversation with Cady Coleman, former NASA Astronaut and author of the forthcoming book, Sharing Space: An Astronaut’s Guide to Mission, Wonder, and Making Change , due out July 2024.
